Influence of water electrolysis on hydrolysis and methanogenesis stages of 
anaerobic digestion at room temperature: Kinetic and metabolic analysis 
Tania Paola Mendoza-Tinoco a, Ulises Dur´an-Hinojosa a, Víctor S´anchez-V´azquez b, María del 
Carmen Fajardo-Ortiz a, Ricardo Beristain-Cardoso d, Ignacio Gonz´alez c,* 
a Departamento de Biotecnología, Universidad Aut´onoma Metropolitana Unidad Iztapalapa, Av. Ferrocarril San Rafael Atlixco, Iztapalapa, 09310 CDMX, Mexico

H I G H L I G H T S  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T  
• A low-magnitude electric field improves 
the AD process by suspended granules. 
• RuO2/Ti favored electrolysis water re­
actions without biofilm formation. 
• The O2 electrochemically generated ac­
celerates the hydrolysis step in AD up to 
72%. 
• O2 stimulates extracellular ORP, modi­
fying anaerobic metabolism. 
• H2 
electrochemically 
generated 
enhanced the methane yield by up to 
39%.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Electric field 
Hydrolysis 
Anaerobic digestion 
Oxygen 
Facultative bacteria 
A B S T R A C T   
Batch cultures were performed to study hydrolysis and methanogenesis in the presence of an electric field at 
room temperature (i.e., 23 ◦C). Kinetic and metabolic analyses using RuO2/Ti electrodes were carried out in short 
reaction times to avoid biofilm formation, allowing the evaluation of the effect of O2 and H2 produced on 
anaerobic digestion during the imposition of three electric fields: 1.21, 1.45, and 1.64 V/cm. Results highlighted 
that at 1.21 V/cm, the electrolysis produced 0.0753 mg O2/L⋅min, where facultative microorganisms consumed 
21 % oxygen, enhancing the hydrolysis phase by 52 %. Additionally, methane production was noticeably 
improved with an activity of 0.89 ± 0.02 g COD-CH4/g VSS⋅d, meaning 39 % higher than the control. The 
imposition of an electric field showed promising results since the methanogenic activity at room temperature was 
very close to the activities observed in conventional reactors at 35 ◦C.

1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) represents a cost-effective and widely 
applied biotechnology to treat high-COD wastewater. It is a complex 
biotechnological process requiring high temperatures (e.g., 35–44 ◦C) to 
achieve high methane yields (Mao et al., 2015), so controlling high 
temperatures in cold climate zones in wastewater treatment plants is 
economically unfeasible. Therefore, developing technologies to operate 
AD at low temperatures while maintaining high yields is a real chal­
lenge, and this is the main goal of the present work. 
Currently, there are some strategies to enhance CH4 yield, but one of 
the most recent is the coupling of electrochemical systems, improving 
COD removal and CH4 production (Mendoza-Tinoco et al., 2023). For 
instance, 0.05 to 3.5 V applied on AD promotes electroactive biofilms on 
the electrode surface, allowing attached bacteria to transfer charges, 
turning them into redox mediators, thus increasing CH4 yield (De Vrieze 
et al., 2018). Koch et al. (2015) imposed a cell potential of 0.2 V, using 
graphite electrodes at 37 ◦C, improving CH4 yield by 27 %. Sun et al. 
(2020) evaluated an anaerobic reactor at HRT of 24 h, with titanium 
mesh electrodes (0.05–0.2 V) at 35 ◦C, observing an increment of 
methane production by 15 % with shifts in the microbial diversity. The 
effect of electrochemical reactions in these systems has been little 
studied, specifically in the granules suspended in the liquid medium. 
Consequently, the intrinsic production of H2 and O2 by the electrolysis of 
water should be one of the variables to consider since AD syntropy al­
lows microorganisms to couple the O2 and H2 produced through elec­
trochemical reactions in their biochemical pathways and, therefore, 
could regulate AD metabolism. For example, Tartakovsky et al. (2011) 
observed an AD improvement by applying a cell potential of 2.8–3.5 V 
for water electrolysis at 35 ◦C; the authors attributed the higher CH4 
yield to the electrochemical production of O2 that favored the hydrolytic 
activity. 
Based on the observations mentioned above, it is necessary to 
develop studies that support the production rate of O2 and H2 and their 
direct effect on each AD stage, mainly in the hydrolysis and methano­
genesis, considered the limiting steps. Therefore, this work aims to 
evaluate the influence of oxygen production by water electrolysis in 
hydrolysis and methanogenesis activities using only granular sludge 
previously stabilized at room temperature in batch cultures. 
2. Materials and methods 
2.1. Inoculum and culture medium 
Anaerobic sludge from a candy-manufacturing wastewater treatment 
plant was stabilized in a laboratory-scale Upflow Anaerobic Sludge 
Blanket (UASB) reactor with an operating volume of 2 L. It was fed with 
the following chemical medium: (in g/L), sucrose (1.5), NH4CI (0.85), 
K2HPO4 (0.234), KH2PO4 (0.136), MgCl⋅6H2O (0.084), NaHCO3 (2), and 
yeast extract (0.34). A trace element solution (0.5 mL/L) was added, 
with the following composition (in g/L), EDTA (0.5), ZnSO4⋅7H2O (0.4), 
CoCl2⋅6H2O (0.25), MnCl2 (0.6), CuSO4⋅5H2O (0.25), Na2MoO4⋅2H2O 
(0.2), NiCl2⋅6H2O (0.2), MgCl2 (0.5), FeSO4 (0.1), and CaCl2⋅2H2O (0.1). 
2.2. Characterization of the bioelectrochemical system for batch cultures 
Electrochemical characterization was performed in glass electro­
chemical reactors (two-electrode cells) with 130 mL of liquid and 10 mL 
of head space. The electrodes were constructed in Ti plates coated with 
RuO2 (RuO2/Ti), whose dimensions were 7.5 cm long, 0.6 cm wide, and 
0.1 cm thick; the submerged area of the electrodes was 9.16 cm2, and the 
separation between electrodes was 2 cm. The electric field is associated 
with the cell potential where two Ti/RuO2 electrodes are immersed in 
the granules and culture medium. A low electric current is imposed, and 
the cell potential developed is monitored with the imposition time. 
Electric field vs. current density curve has been used to find an operating 
interval in which a resistive behavior was observed to ensure no 
chemical alterations in the culture chemical composition (G´omez-Flores 
et al., 2020). A high-precision power supply (BK PRECISIONS Model 
9120A, Taiwan) was used to apply the electric current. A voltammetric 
study was carried out with a mineral medium containing sucrose and 
acetate. A voltammogram from −1 to 1.7 V with a scan potential of 10 
mV/s was performed (in a three-cell electrode) by using mercury/mer­
curous sulfate/saturated sulfate (SSE) and a carbon cylinder as reference 
and counter electrodes, respectively. 
2.3. Characterization of the anaerobic digestion stages applying an 
electric field 
Batch cultures were inoculated with 2 g VSS/L previously acclima­
tized in the UASB. Experimental units were bubbled with N2 for 3 min to 
ensure an oxygen-free environment. Initially, batch cultures (without an 
electric field) were carried out as a control assay. Subsequently, the 
effect of the electric field on hydrolysis and methanogenesis was eval­
uated by applying three magnitudes (1.21, 1.45, and 1.64 V/cm). In the 
hydrolysis culture, sucrose was used as a carbon source at 0.9 g/L, where 
sucrose consumption was monitored over time. In the methanogenic 
culture, 1.5 g/L acetic acid was added; where methane production was 
plotted, and the specific methanogenic activity (SMA) was determined. 
Origin Pro Software was used to calculate the kinetic parameters using 
the Gompertz Model. A single-factor analysis of variance (ANOVA) was 
performed to compare the experimental results obtained in the presence 
and absence of an electric field. The significance value (α) was 5 % using 
the data analysis add-in of Microsoft Excel software. 
2.4. Determination of O2 production and facultative activity 
In batch cultures, the dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration was 
quantified in the presence and absence of an electric field; this consisted 
of applying the three selected electric field magnitudes. Abiotic (without 
sludge) and biotic (with 2 g VSS/L of sludge) experiments were per­
formed with constant stirring at 100 rpm for five hours. The O2 con­
sumption capacity of the sludge was determined in independent 
experiments in which air was supplied by bubbling until a pseudo- 
stationary state was reached; once a constant concentration was 
reached, aeration was stopped, and the DO consumption profile was 
monitored. The consumption kinetics were established and adjusted to a 
Monod-type model to determine the O2 consumption capacity of the 
facultative microorganisms. 
2.5. Analytical methods 
pH was measured with a multiparameter (Orion Star™ A215, 
Indonesia). ORP was measured with a selective electrode (Cole-Parmer 
EW-27009-30) connected to a pH/ORP controller meter (Eutech In­
struments 800, Singapore). Phenol–sulfuric acid and DNS techniques 
were used to quantify total and reducing sugars, respectively. Volatile 
fatty acids were quantified in a gas chromatograph (Agilent Technolo­
gies 7820A, Shanghai) with a flame ignition detector (FID), using N2 as a 
carrier gas, with a heating ramp from 80 ◦C to 200 ◦C, with increments of 
25 ◦C/min, with an Agilent J&W DB-FFAP column. The biogas compo­
sition was determined using helium as the carrier gas with a gas chro­
matograph (Gow-Mac 580 GC, U.S. A) with a thermal conductivity 
detector (TCD). The operating conditions were as follows: Tcolumn =
40 ◦C, Tinjector = 90 ◦C, Tdetector = 90 ◦C, detector current: 120 mA. The 
DO was quantified with the sensor based on the phenomenon of pho­
toluminescence (WTW™ FDO 925, Germany).

3. Results and discussion 
3.1. Characterization of the bioelectrochemical system 
Cell potential versus applied current density curves were constructed 
to determine a current density interval in which the media behaves like 
an electrical resistance (see Supplementary material). Electrical resis­
tance behavior allows the operation to ensure that the electrochemical 
reactions on the surface of the electrodes will not alter the chemical 
composition of the medium (G´omez-Flores et al., 2020). The resistive 
behavior was found by applying an interval of 0.54 to 1.63 mA/cm2 
(Supplementary material); the electric field magnitudes applied to the 
cell were 1.21, 1.45 and 1.64 V/cm.). The voltammogram obtained in a 
mineral medium containing sucrose and acetate showed neither reduc­
tion nor oxidation of any chemical component in the culture medium; 
only water electrolysis reactions occurred at the anodic and cathodic 
potential barriers (see Supplementary material). 
3.2. Effect of the electric field on the hydrolysis stage 
The consumption profile of sucrose in the control study was 
consumed at five hours, while the studies with the imposition of 1.21, 
1.45, and 1.64 V/cm reached it at approximately 4 h (Fig. 1a). The 
electric field effect was reflected in the hydrolysis efficiencies, which 
when compared at 3 h, the control had a hydrolysis efficiency of 68 ±
1.42 %. In contrast, in the applied electric fields of 1.21, 1.45, and 1.64 
V/cm, the hydrolysis efficiencies obtained were 91 ± 0.28 %, 83 ± 0.20 
%, and 93 ± 1.18 %, respectively. 
The kinetic analysis revealed that the reaction constant increased 
compared to the control by 52, 42, and 72 % for electric field magni­
tudes of 1.21, 1.45, and 1.64 V/cm, respectively (Table 1). These results 
indicated that the characteristic time of the hydrolysis stage decreases 
with increases in the electric field, which could improve the AD’s overall 
performance. Tartakovsky et al. (2011) suggested that microaerobic

conditions by water electrolysis might favor the proliferation of facul­
tative bacteria with better hydrolytic activities due to aerobic routes. On 
the other hand, Zhang et al. (2021) indicated that microaerobic condi­
tions might increase extracellular enzyme production, speeding up the 
organic matter hydrolysis. 
In abiotic experiments, three electric field magnitudes were applied 
to support the previous proposals, reaching similar oxygen saturation 
concentrations (Fig. 2a). However, the production rate increased pro­
portionally to the magnitude of the electric field: 0.0753, 0.0822, and 
0.0943 mg O2/L⋅min for 1.21, 1.45, and 1.64 V/cm, respectively 
(Fig. 2a-c). In biotic experiments, DO is consumed almost entirely, in 
which the lowest concentration of DO was obtained at 1.21 V/cm 
(Fig. 2a). The data obtained in the biotic system (previously saturated 
with O2) in the absence of the electric field (Fig. 2d) showed a maximum 
oxygen consumption rate of 0.484 ± 0.049 mg O2/L⋅min with an affinity 
constant of 0.877 ± 0.222 mg/L. Based on these values, the oxygen 
consumption rates were estimated at 0.016 ± 0.002, 0.123 ± 0.020, and 
0.154 ± 0.012 mg O2/L⋅min for the applied electric fields of 1.21, 1.45, 
and 1.64 V/cm, respectively. These results show how, from 200 min, the 
DO begins to accumulate in the aqueous stage with 1.45 and 1.64 V/cm 
since the capability of microorganisms to consume O2 is overwhelmed 
(Fig. 2b-c). At the same time, when 1.21 V/cm was applied, facultative 
bacteria maintained a microaerobic environment with a concentration 
of 0.04 ± 0.01 mg/L (Fig. 2a). Therefore, it can be concluded that the 
electric field decreases the characteristic time for the hydrolysis stage, 
which is attributed to the fact that the electrochemically generated ox­
ygen favors the metabolism of facultative bacteria. 
On the other hand, in all batch cultures, pH values were within the 
range of 7.2 to 7.7, an acceptable value for anaerobic digestion. The ORP 
in the hydrolysis stage displayed less negative values in the presence of 
the electric field, and this behavior was proportional to the increase in 
electric field magnitude (Fig. 1b). The profiles were stabilized from hour 
two and remained constant until hour five; the control presented a value 
of −272 ± 11.3 mV, while the electric field presented values of −251 ±
0.7, −229 ± 3.5 and −226 ± 2.8 mV for electric field magnitudes of 
1.21, 1.45 and 1.64 V/cm, respectively. 
3.3. Effect of the electric field on the methanogenesis stage 
Batch cultures fed with acetic acid to evaluate methanogenic activity 
showed that the three tests performed with an electric field display an 
adaptation stage at one hour with a methane production of 12.5 ± 2.5 
mL (Fig. 1c). In contrast, the control showed a higher methane pro­
duction in the first hour of 32.5 mL ± 2.1. Methanogens are the most 
susceptible to oxygen because they cannot synthesize the superoxide 
dismutase enzyme that aerobic organisms use to neutralize reactive 
oxygen species. However, in the presence of O2 to overcome oxidative 
stress, some methanogenic species may have intrinsic tolerance to ox­
ygen exposure as they adapt to environmental conditions and can even 
produce superoxide dismutase, which could explain how these experi­
ments showed this adaptive stage (Magdalena et al., 2022). 
On the other hand, the control presented a SMA value of 0.64 ±
0.003 g COD-CH4/g VSS⋅d; this agrees with data reported in the litera­
ture (Gonzalez-Tineo et al., 2020). At the same time, assays in the

presence of an electric field were 0.89 ± 0.02, 0.44 ± 0.05, and 0.13 ±
0.001 g COD-CH4/g VSS⋅d for magnitudes of electric fields of 1.21, 1.45, 
and 1.64 V/cm, respectively; the batch cultures performed at 1.21 V/cm 
presented an increase of 39 % compared to the control. 
Most known methanogenic archaea are mesophilic and have an op­
timum temperature of 35 ◦C, diminishing the SMA when temperature is 
dropped. For example, Kayranli and Ugurlu (2012) using acetate ob­
tained a SMA of 0.74 g COD/g VSS⋅d at 25 ◦C, 0.70 g COD/g VSS⋅d at 
15 ◦C, and 0.68 g COD/g VSS-d at 10 ◦C, in comparison with the research 
of Soto et al. (1993), who observed an SMA between 1.078 and 0.975 g 
COD/g VSS⋅d at 35 ◦C. In the present study, the SMA exceeds the value 
reported at 25 ◦C, meaning that the electric field enhances this biological 
process, competing successfully with conventional AD at 35 ◦C. 
Finally, 1.21 and 1.45 V/cm of electric fields did not affect the 
reducing conditions since the ORP was similar to the culture control, 
maintaining values of −277.33 ± 2.1 to −302.5 ± 2.8 mV from hours 
two to five (Fig. 1d). However, at 1.64 V/cm, the ORP was less negative 
regarding the control, with an average value of −120.08 ± 7.2 from 
hours two to seven. Nghiem et al. (2014) reported that microaeration in 
an anaerobic digester changed the ORP to less negative values, from 
−485 mV to −270 mV. 
4. Conclusions 
By conducting water electrolysis caused by a low-magnitude electric 
field at 23 ◦C, the outcome of anaerobic digestion was strongly 
impacted. The micro-aerobic conditions enhanced the hydrolysis rate of 
sucrose at any electric field, thus improving the organic matter removal. 
The microbial methanogenic activity was positively stimulated at the 
lowest electric field since acetate consumption was increased with a 
concomitantly enhanced methane production; real matrix will be used 
to validate the positive effect of the electric field. These findings open an 
alternative to significant development using a controlled low-magnitude 
electric field to redirect the desired products without temperature 
control.
